werk/dashboard-confessional-the-swiss-ar.text:
The Swiss Army Romance is the debut album by Dashboard Confessional, released in March 2000 on Fiddler Records and limited to a thousand copies. Shortly afterwards it was decided to sell the album to Drive-Thru Records, which reissued it on 14 November 2000. Chris Carrabba wrote all the songs, sang and played guitar. James Paul Wisner produced the record and played keyboards. John Ralston added guitar and backing vocals.

In 2003 the rights were sold to Carrabba and Vagrant Records, and the record was reissued with the bonus tracks Hold On and This Is a Forgery. The reasons were the band's growing popularity and the approaching album A Mark, a Mission, a Brand, a Scar. Rock Sound ranked the album number 100 in its list of 101 Modern Classics, and Loudwire included it in a list of the best emo albums.
werk/dashboard-confessional-the-swiss-ar.listen: Listen to Screaming Infidelities and notice the voice and guitar of Chris Carrabba, who wrote all the songs.

werk/dave-brubeck-brubeck-a-la-mode.text:
This 1960 studio album consists almost entirely of compositions by the clarinettist Bill Smith. It was one of three albums the quartet made with Smith. Besides the pianist Dave Brubeck, the bassist Eugene Wright and the drummer Joe Morello play on it.

The cover is striking: the quartet sit laughing and eating ice cream at an ice-cream parlour. The author Todd R. Decker places that image in the context of the civil rights movement, with the sit-ins at lunch counters in Greensboro and Nashville. The music received a mixed reception. Scott Yanow of AllMusic felt that the music swings and that there are good solos, but that no single piece is truly memorable. Billboard wrote in January 1961 that the music is swinging and lively.
werk/dave-brubeck-brubeck-a-la-mode.listen: In Frisco Fog, at just over six minutes the longest track on the album, listen to the interplay between clarinet and piano.

werk/dave-brubeck-quartet-dave-digs-disn.text:
Dave Digs Disney is a 1957 studio album by the Dave Brubeck Quartet, with jazz versions of songs from the Disney films Alice in Wonderland, Pinocchio and Snow White. The quartet had been playing Disney songs live now and then for some time, but it took a family visit to Disneyland to convince the pianist to phone his producer with the idea for a whole album. Disney music was then regarded as light pop, beneath the level of jazz musicians. He took a financial risk, and it paid off well.

Paul Desmond plays alto saxophone, Joe Morello drums and Norman Bates bass. The original LP was released in mono only, although stereo tapes also existed. Some Day My Prince Will Come became a jazz standard, later recorded by Miles Davis and John Coltrane, among others. Other jazz musicians followed with Disney songs. It is one of the quartet's most popular albums.
werk/dave-brubeck-quartet-dave-digs-disn.listen: Listen to Some Day My Prince Will Come and notice how the jazz musicians use the familiar film song as a starting point for their playing.

werk/dave-brubeck-quartet-gone-with-the-.text:
In 1959 the Dave Brubeck Quartet wanted to make an album of their own music in unusual time signatures, which the group had come to know while travelling, for example in Turkish folk music. That became Time Out. The label's management, however, demanded that the band first make a more conventional record, to cover the risk. This is how Gone With the Wind came about, recorded on 22 and 23 April 1959 in Los Angeles.

It is a concept album paying tribute to the state of Georgia and the American South. Eugene Wright chose Ol' Man River and Joe Morello Short'nin' Bread. Paul Desmond chose The Lonesome Road and Basin Street Blues. Dave Brubeck took Georgia on My Mind and Swanee River. Critics called the album everything you would expect from Brubeck, and the most swinging the group had recorded up to that point. It was also seen as one of the weaker records by this classic line-up. Time Out later achieved the status of a milestone.
werk/dave-brubeck-quartet-gone-with-the-.listen: In Georgia on My Mind, listen to Brubeck's piano; he chose this piece for the album himself.

werk/dave-brubeck-quartet-time-out.text:
The album was intended as an experiment with rhythms the quartet had come to know on a tour of Eurasia sponsored by the US State Department. In Turkey, Dave Brubeck heard street musicians playing a folk tune in 9/8, divided as 2+2+2+3. Columbia president Goddard Lieberson took a gamble, financing Time Out and releasing it in 1959, after the quartet had first recorded a conventional album.

The theme is unusual time signatures. Blue Rondo à la Turk begins in 9/8, Take Five stays in 5/4 throughout and Three to Get Ready alternates between 3/4 and 4/4. Take Five was written by the alto saxophonist Paul Desmond, the only title not by the pianist; he said it was really meant to be a drum solo for Joe Morello. The album became the first jazz record to sell a million copies. In 2005 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry.
werk/dave-brubeck-quartet-time-out.listen: In Take Five, listen to the constantly recurring five-beat bar in the rhythm and to Joe Morello's drum solo.

werk/dave-holland-emerald-tears.text:
Dave Holland recorded this solo album in August 1977 and released it the following year on the ECM label. It is a record full of bass solos: only a single double bass is heard, with no accompaniment from other musicians. The eight pieces show what a bassist can do on his own with tone and rhythm.

The critical response was positive. AllMusic called it a fine showcase for Holland, one that would appeal above all to lovers of the upright bass. DownBeat gave the album three and a half stars and praised his rich, polished tone and his throbbing, percussive sensitivity, with a melancholy, romantic touch. The reviewer did feel, however, that the album at times seemed like a Music Minus One record turned inside out.
werk/dave-holland-emerald-tears.listen: Listen to Emerald Tears and notice how a single unaccompanied double bass can carry melody and rhythm at the same time.

werk/dave-holland-life-cycle.text:
Life Cycle is a solo album for cello, recorded in November 1982 and released a year later on ECM. Dave Holland is known above all as a bassist. Here he plays a different instrument, and for many listeners that is a lesser-known side of his musical talent. Manfred Eicher produced the album and Martin Wieland recorded it.

The album opens with Inception and contains a series of pieces under the title Life Cycle, called Discovery, Longing, Search and Resolution. These are followed by, among others, Sonnet, Rune, Troubadour Tale, Grapevine, Morning Song and Chanson Pour La Nuit. In his review for AllMusic, Brian Olewnick wrote of an enchanting solo concert for cello and recommended the album.
werk/dave-holland-life-cycle.listen: Listen to the four parts of Life Cycle in a row and notice how the cello takes on a different character from Discovery to Resolution.

werk/dave-liebman-drum-ode.text:
Drum Ode was recorded in May 1974 and released a year later on ECM. The saxophonist Dave Liebman assembled a group of thirteen musicians: the guitarist John Abercrombie, the pianist Richard Beirach, the bassist Gene Perla, the singer Eleana Steinberg and above all eight percussionists, among them Bob Moses, Jeff Williams, Barry Altschul, Badal Roy and Collin Walcott. Liebman plays soprano and tenor saxophone and alto flute.

The programme opens with Goli Dance, a traditional piece lasting only half a minute, and includes original pieces by Liebman, among them Loft Dance and The Iguana's Ritual. Your Lady is by John Coltrane. The Penguin Guide to Jazz included the record in its Core Collection and AllMusic gave it three stars.
werk/dave-liebman-drum-ode.listen: In Loft Dance, listen to the many percussionists and notice how the rhythms weave in and out of one another.

werk/dave-van-ronk-folksinger.text:
After his appearance at the Newport Jazz Festival and tours of America, Chess Records urged Muddy Waters to record a new studio album. Because folk was popular at the time, the label chose the title Folk Singer and had an acoustic album made with two acoustic guitarists. It was recorded in September 1963 at the Ter Mar Recording Studios in Chicago, with Willie Dixon as producer and on double bass. Buddy Guy played as second guitarist.

It is the bluesman's only fully acoustic album and sounds very different from his earlier, electric work. Most of the songs go at a leisurely pace, and he underlines his singing with hums and sighs. In 1964 reviewers were divided, but later it received much praise, especially for its intimate, clear sound. Rolling Stone called the acoustic playing groundbreaking.
werk/dave-van-ronk-folksinger.listen: Listen to Good Morning Little School Girl, the only song that goes faster than the rest. Notice how the two acoustic guitars complement each other and how the voice moves between them.

werk/david-arnold-shaken-and-stirred-the.text:
In 1997 David Arnold put this album together: a collection of covers of James Bond themes, sung and played by contemporary rock and electronica artists. It was released on East West in the United Kingdom and on Sire in the United States. After this project Arnold would go on to compose the music for several Bond films.

John Barry, the composer of many of the themes, was complimentary: Arnold stayed true to the melody and harmony but added fresh rhythms and interesting choices of artists. Thus David McAlmont sings Diamonds Are Forever and Arnold works with Propellerheads on On Her Majesty's Secret Service. Both tracks were released as singles in the United Kingdom. A version of You Only Live Twice with Björk was recorded but did not make the record. The album reached number eleven in the UK albums chart.
werk/david-arnold-shaken-and-stirred-the.listen: Listen to On Her Majesty's Secret Service and notice what Propellerheads add to the Bond theme: which elements sound contemporary, and which melody do you recognise from the original?

werk/david-bowie-aladdin-sane.text:
After his breakthrough with Ziggy Stardust, David Bowie wrote an album for the first time as an established star. He made most of the songs during the American tour at the end of 1972, and America leaves a clear mark on it. Bowie himself described it as Ziggy goes to America. He recorded it in New York and London between legs of the tour, with the producer Ken Scott and the Spiders from Mars, for the last time with the full line-up.

The pianist Mike Garson, with a background in jazz and blues, added something new to the arrangements. The lyrics deal with urban decay, drugs, sex, violence and death. The sound is harder than before, with influences from the Rolling Stones, one of whose songs is covered. The Jean Genie and Drive-In Saturday reached the British top five, and the album went to number one in England. Critics were positive.
werk/david-bowie-aladdin-sane.listen: In Time, listen to Mike Garson's piano part, and notice how it gives the song a different colour from what the rock line-up alone would have done.

werk/david-bowie-diamond-dogs.text:
After Pin Ups, David Bowie was not sure where his career was heading. He had disbanded the Spiders from Mars and parted company with the producer Ken Scott. He had several plans: a musical based on Ziggy Stardust, an adaptation of Nineteen Eighty-Four by George Orwell and an apocalyptic city story after William S. Burroughs. Orwell's widow refused the rights, and the musical never happened. What remained was recorded in London and the Netherlands in early 1974.

Bowie produced the record himself and, in the absence of Mick Ronson, also played lead guitar. Tony Visconti returned for the string arrangements and the mix. The sound is raw and slightly clumsy, and it was his last glam rock album. Rebel Rebel was released ahead of it as a single. Critics missed coherence, but the record went to number one in the United Kingdom.
werk/david-bowie-diamond-dogs.listen: Listen to Rebel Rebel and notice the guitar riff that carries the song, played in that raw sound which gives the record its own flavour.

werk/david-bowie-heroes.text:
After Low, released in early 1977 with hardly any promotion, David Bowie recorded Iggy Pop's Lust for Life in Berlin in May and June. After that he was ready for a new record of his own. Together with Brian Eno and the producer Tony Visconti, he settled in Hansa Studio 2, a former concert hall about five hundred metres from the Berlin Wall. Visconti said that the threatening atmosphere made the band play with a great deal of energy. The guitarist Robert Fripp was brought in on Eno's suggestion.

Most of the music was created on the spot in the studio, and Bowie wrote the lyrics only in front of the microphone. The record builds on the electronic and ambient approach of Low, but sounds more positive. The first side contains straightforward rock songs, the second mostly instrumental pieces. The title song was at first not a success as a single, but grew into one of his best known.
werk/david-bowie-heroes.listen: Listen to "Heroes" and notice the guitar of Robert Fripp, which plays a prominent part in the song.

werk/david-bowie-hunky-dory.text:
After The Man Who Sold the World, David Bowie was inactive for a time, without a band and with a new manager. He began writing songs, now on piano rather than guitar. In 1971 he recorded the album at Trident Studios in London, with Mick Ronson on guitar, Trevor Bolder on bass and Mick Woodmansey on drums. Rick Wakeman played piano, shortly before joining Yes. Ken Scott co-produced.

The sound is warmer and more melodic than on the guitar-heavy album before it. Changes is about the compulsion towards artistic renewal. After a tour of America the singer wrote songs for Andy Warhol, Bob Dylan and Lou Reed, and Kooks for his newborn son Duncan. RCA hardly promoted the album, so it sold poorly at first and did not make the charts. After the success of Ziggy Stardust in 1972 there was renewed interest. Now it is regarded as the album on which he found his own voice.
werk/david-bowie-hunky-dory.listen: In Changes, listen to the lyrics about the need to keep reinventing yourself.

werk/david-bowie-low.text:
After years of cocaine addiction, David Bowie moved to France in 1976 together with Iggy Pop. Recording began in September 1976 at the Château d'Hérouville and ended in October at Hansa Studios in West Berlin. It was the first of three collaborations with the producer Tony Visconti and Brian Eno, the Berlin Trilogy. German groups such as Tangerine Dream, Neu!, Harmonia and Kraftwerk were an influence.

The first side consists of short, direct song fragments with mostly bleak lyrics. The second side has longer, mainly instrumental pieces, intended as musical impressions of Berlin. Visconti created the characteristic drum sound with an Eventide Harmonizer. The record company held the record back for three months for fear of a flop. Critics were divided, but later it was regarded as one of the singer's best albums. Many post-punk bands were influenced by it.
werk/david-bowie-low.listen: Listen to Sound and Vision and notice the drum sound, which was processed with a harmonizer.

werk/david-bowie-pin-ups.text:
Pin Ups came out in 1973, soon after Aladdin Sane. The record company RCA wanted a new album for Christmas and David Bowie, exhausted after the Ziggy Stardust Tour, came up with a stopgap of covers of bands that had influenced him as a teenager. At the last show of the tour he had unexpectedly announced that it would be the last, which caused tension with the Spiders from Mars. Mick Ronson and Trevor Bolder took part, and the drummer Aynsley Dunbar replaced Woody Woodmansey. Recording took three weeks, in the summer of 1973 at the Château d'Hérouville in France, with Ken Scott as co-producer.

The selection contains songs by the Pretty Things, the Who, the Yardbirds, the Kinks and Pink Floyd, such as See Emily Play and Shapes of Things. The arrangements stay close to the originals, but sound like glam rock and proto-punk. The record went to the top of the British albums chart, but critics mostly found the covers inferior to the originals.
werk/david-bowie-pin-ups.listen: In See Emily Play, listen to the arrangement, which differs from Pink Floyd's original, while most of the covers on the record stay close to theirs.

werk/david-bowie-station-to-station.text:
Station to Station was released on 23 January 1976 on RCA. David Bowie recorded it in late 1975, mostly at Cherokee Studios in Los Angeles, after the filming of The Man Who Fell to Earth. He was plagued by drug addiction at the time and later remembered almost nothing of the sessions. The success of Young Americans gave him time and room. He came to the studio with loose ideas, and the guitarist Carlos Alomar, the bassist George Murray and the drummer Dennis Davis worked them out. Those three formed his rhythm section for the rest of the decade.

The album builds on the funk and soul of Young Americans, but also looks to the German krautrock of Neu! and Kraftwerk. The lyrics deal with Nietzsche, Aleister Crowley and mythology. Golden Years was released ahead of it as a single. During the sessions Frank Sinatra praised the recording of Wild Is the Wind, which Bowie made as a tribute to Nina Simone.
werk/david-bowie-station-to-station.listen: Listen to Wild Is the Wind, the closing track. Bowie recorded this cover as a tribute to Nina Simone: notice how he sings the song.

werk/david-bowie-the-man-who-sold-the-wo.text:
The Man Who Sold the World is David Bowie's third studio album. It was released on 4 November 1970 in the United States and on 8 April 1971 in the United Kingdom. Tony Visconti produced the record, which was recorded in London in April and May 1970. The guitarist Mick Ronson and the drummer Mick Woodmansey play here for the first time, later members of the Spiders from Mars. After the acoustic previous album he opted for hard rock with blues rock and much darker lyrics about madness, religion, technology and war.

Ronson and Visconti arranged most of it, because the singer was busy with his new marriage and with management matters. No singles were released. The American cover shows a cowboy in front of an asylum, the British one a man in a blue dress. Commercially it was a failure, but later it was praised for the band's playing and its unsettling atmosphere. Many see it as the start of his classic period.
werk/david-bowie-the-man-who-sold-the-wo.listen: Listen to The Width of a Circle and notice how hard and heavy the band sounds here, very different from the acoustic album before it.

werk/david-bowie-young-americans.text:
After Diamond Dogs, David Bowie's last glam rock album, he wanted to go fully for soul music. Recording began in August 1974 at Sigma Sound Studios in Philadelphia, the home of Philadelphia soul, and lasted two weeks. The producer Tony Visconti led the sessions. The guitarist Carlos Alomar became a regular collaborator and Luther Vandross, still unknown then, sang backing vocals. A large part of the music was recorded live with the whole band. In January 1975 a session followed in New York with John Lennon, producing Across the Universe and Fame.

He himself called the sound plastic soul, while critics speak of blue-eyed soul. Fame became his first number one single and the album brought his breakthrough in the United States, with a place in the top ten. Reviews were mixed, but the record became influential, because he was one of the first white artists of the time to engage openly with new Black styles.
werk/david-bowie-young-americans.listen: In Young Americans, listen to how the full band with backing singers creates a soul sound together, and notice how live it sounds.

werk/david-bowie-ziggy-stardust.text:
After the American promotional tour of February 1971, David Bowie wrote more than thirty new songs in England. Some ended up on Hunky Dory, the rest on this album. It was recorded from November 1971 to February 1972 at Trident Studios in London, with Ken Scott as co-producer and the Spiders from Mars as the band: Mick Ronson on guitar, Trevor Bolder on bass and Mick Woodmansey on drums. Many songs were recorded almost live.

It is a loose concept album about Ziggy Stardust, an androgynous rock star who comes to earth as a saviour and is brought down by his own ego. The story largely emerged only after the songs had been recorded. The music is glam rock with influences from Marc Bolan, Iggy Pop and the Velvet Underground. After the performance of Starman on Top of the Pops in July 1972 he broke through. Later critics see the record as his peak.
werk/david-bowie-ziggy-stardust.listen: Listen to Moonage Daydream and notice how Mick Ronson's guitar carries the song alongside the vocals. Can you hear how the band sounds like one group playing together?

werk/david-byrne-american-utopia.text:
David Byrne released American Utopia in March 2018, his first solo album since Grown Backwards in 2004. He wrote it together with Brian Eno, who wrote eight of the ten songs and played on four of them. The record belongs to the multimedia project Reasons to Be Cheerful, which offers reasons to remain optimistic despite political tensions and environmental problems. The title comes from a song by Ian Dury. The first single was Everybody's Coming to My House.

The album then grew into a complete theatre project. On tour Byrne stood on an empty stage surrounded by chains, with twelve barefoot musicians in grey suits. They played without cables, with choreography by Annie-B Parson. A Broadway show, a film by Spike Lee and a picture book followed later. The reactions were mostly positive, and it became his first top ten album in the American charts.
werk/david-byrne-american-utopia.listen: In Everybody's Coming To My House, the first single, listen to the vocals and the rhythm. Notice how the music sets the mood of an invitation.

werk/david-byrne-rei-momo.text:
Rei Momo was released on 3 October 1989 and was David Byrne's first real solo album. Before that, in 1981, he had already made the collaborative album My Life in the Bush of Ghosts. The record came out on Luaka Bop and Sire. Three songs, Loco de Amor, Good and Evil and Office Cowboy, were not on the LP, but were on the cassette and CD.

The album contains many different Latin American styles: rumba, mambo, cha-cha-chá and bolero from Cuba, merengue from the Dominican Republic, bomba from Puerto Rico, cumbia from Colombia and samba from Brazil. Even so, the singing is mainly in English. Kirsty MacColl, Willie Colón and Celia Cruz, among others, appear as guests. Byrne played Dirty Old Town and Loco de Amor on Saturday Night Live in 1989. Critics were positive. Alexis Petridis later called the record an underrated joy in The Guardian.
werk/david-byrne-rei-momo.listen: Listen to Make Believe Mambo and notice how the Latin American rhythms carry the song while Byrne sings over them in English.

werk/david-byrne-the-forest.text:
The Forest was released in June 1991 and is a largely instrumental album by David Byrne. It is inspired by the Epic of Gilgamesh and is set in the period of the late Industrial Revolution. Part of this orchestral music was first used in a theatre piece of the same name, directed by Robert Wilson. That piece premiered in 1988 at the Theater der Freien Volksbühne in West Berlin.

After the record, Forestry also appeared, a maxi single with dance and industrial remixes of pieces from the album. Jack Dangers, Rudy Tambala and Anthony Capel made those remixes, including of Ava and Nineveh. The cover shows no forest, but an industrial photograph of pipes and a pump, in keeping with the theme of the album.
werk/david-byrne-the-forest.listen: Listen to Ava and notice that this is not a song with vocals, but an instrumental piece that is above all about the sound of the instruments.

werk/david-byrne-uh-oh.text:
Uh-Oh was David Byrne's second studio album, in 1992. Nick Launay produced it. The cover shows angels around a cartoon dog, a nod to the word god spelled backwards. For the record the singer worked with a large group of musicians, including brass, strings and percussionists, with Angel Fernandez as arranger.

The sound is full of Latin American influences. The Orlando Sentinel felt the Afro-Brazilian influences were better integrated than on Rei Momo from 1989. The New York Times wrote that he had finally made the Pan-American dance album he had been seeking since the mid-1980s. The Guardian called it his most Talking Heads-like solo record. The song She's Mad reached number three on the Modern Rock chart.
werk/david-byrne-uh-oh.listen: In She's Mad, listen to how the rhythms and the horns lay a danceable foundation, while the vocals sit nervously on top.

werk/david-cassidy-cherish.text:
David Cassidy had become famous through the TV series The Partridge Family. The producer Wes Farrell wanted to detach him from that series as a solo star. He therefore recorded an album in the second half of 1971 with almost the same musicians and engineers as on the earlier Partridge Family records, but with a more mature sound and more personal material. Tony Romeo and Adam Miller each wrote three songs, and Kin Vassy supplied the dramatic ballad My First Night Alone Without You. Ricky's Tune was written by the singer himself.

The title song was a cover of a 1966 hit by The Association and became the first solo single. The album was released in early 1972 on Bell Records. In the United States it reached number 15 on the Billboard 200. In the United Kingdom it even reached number 2, and there began a period in which he was one of the biggest teen idols. Later the album received mostly positive reviews.
werk/david-cassidy-cherish.listen: Listen to I Am a Clown and notice the spoken introduction at the start: how does the tone of his voice change when the song itself begins?

werk/david-cassidy-dreams-are-nuthin-mor.text:
Dreams Are Nuthin' More Than Wishes is David Cassidy's third solo album, released in 1973 by Bell Records and produced by Rick Jarrard. It consists mostly of covers, including Daydream by John Sebastian, Fever by Peggy Lee and The Puppy Song by Nilsson. The album title comes from that last one. He also sang his own version of Summer Days, a song by The Partridge Family.

The gatefold sleeve and the handwritten notes, in which he explains why he chose each song, are distinctive. The album reached number one on the British albums chart in 1973 and made the Australian top twenty in 1974, during his tour there. A reviewer called the record an album to melt the icicles from the heart of every little girl, and praised the sequencing, in which his charm came across well.
werk/david-cassidy-dreams-are-nuthin-mor.listen: Listen to Daydream and notice the harmonica in the arrangement.

werk/david-cassidy-gettin-it-in-the-stre.text:
Gettin' It in the Street is David Cassidy's sixth studio album and his third and last for RCA. Gerry Beckley of America co-produced and co-wrote several of the songs. In November 1976 the record was released in Germany and Japan, but it did not make the album charts. RCA had also pressed copies for the American market, but did not release them officially. Only in 1979 did they turn up in the bargain bins.

Mick Ronson played lead guitar on the title song, which as a single reached number seven in the readers' chart of the German teen magazine Bravo. Cruise to Harlem was co-written by Brian Wilson, founder of the Beach Boys. Stephen Thomas Erlewine of AllMusic called the record, despite its lack of success, one of the singer's best: pleasant, breezy mainstream pop from the mid-1970s.
werk/david-cassidy-gettin-it-in-the-stre.listen: Listen to Gettin' It in the Street and notice the lead guitar of Mick Ronson.

werk/david-cassidy-rock-me-baby.text:
After his debut Cherish, David Cassidy wanted to leave his teen image behind. On his second solo album, produced in 1972 by Wes Farrell for Bell Records, rock, soul and R&B therefore came to the fore. According to AllMusic, Farrell was officially the producer, but the choice of songs and styles showed that the singer also had a say himself. He wrote Two Time Loser and wrote Song for a Rainy Day together with Kim Carnes.

The album opens with the title song, a robust dip into glam rock, which reached the top 40 in the United States. The cover of How Can I Be Sure, originally by the Young Rascals, did even better and spent two weeks at number 1 in the United Kingdom. The album itself reached number 41 in the American chart and rose to number 2 in England. In 2003 it was released on CD by Arista.
werk/david-cassidy-rock-me-baby.listen: Listen to the opening song Rock Me Baby and notice how hard and direct the band sounds, and compare that with the softer pop sound of How Can I Be Sure.

werk/david-hasselhoff-crazy-for-you.text:
Crazy for You was released in August 1990 and is the fourth studio album by the American actor and singer. The producer Jack White, with whom he had worked since 1988, also led this album. Their collaboration had begun with Looking for Freedom, a big hit in Europe that spent eight weeks at number one in Germany. During the promotion of the album that followed, Hasselhoff was already recording new songs.

Besides White, Charles Blackwell, Mark Spiro and Diane Warren, among others, co-wrote. The title song, Freedom for the World and Let's Dance Tonight were released as singles. The album did particularly well in Europe: it reached number one in Austria and Switzerland and became the best-selling album of his career.
werk/david-hasselhoff-crazy-for-you.listen: Listen to Crazy for You, the title song with which the album was promoted, and notice how polished Jack White's production sounds.

werk/david-hasselhoff-looking-for-freedo.text:
Looking for Freedom is Hasselhoff's third studio album and was released on 21 June 1989 on White Records. His first two records, Night Rocker and Lovin' Feelings, were successful in Europe thanks to Knight Rider. After his first tour of Austria in 1987 he began working with the German producer Jack White. Their first collaboration was the title song, which Marc Seaberg had already recorded in 1978.

Looking for Freedom spent eight weeks at number one in Germany and became his biggest hit in Germany, Switzerland and Austria. Is Everybody Happy followed as the second single. He also sang the title song at the Berlin Wall on New Year's Eve 1989. The album itself reached the top five in Germany and Austria and the top three in Switzerland. Later that year a version appeared under the title Lonely Is the Night, with ten of the thirteen songs.
werk/david-hasselhoff-looking-for-freedo.listen: Listen to Looking for Freedom and notice how the chorus is built so that you can sing along quickly.

werk/david-hasselhoff-night-rocker.text:
Night Rocker is the debut album of the American actor David Hasselhoff. It was released in January 1985 on Silver Blue Records and produced by Joel Diamond. On the front he sits on the bonnet of a black Pontiac Firebird, the same car as KITT from the series Knight Rider in which he starred, with a guitar in his hands.

Three songs are duets with Catherine Hickland: Our First Night Together, No Way to Be in Love and Let It Be Me. All three could be heard in the episode of Knight Rider titled Let It Be Me. In this way the record was closely tied to his television work. The album reached number one in Austria and was certified platinum there. In Germany it also reached the top thirty.
werk/david-hasselhoff-night-rocker.listen: Listen to Our First Night Together and notice how his voice and that of Catherine Hickland alternate.

werk/david-sanborn-as-we-speak.text:
As We Speak was released in 1982 on Warner Bros. Records. Robert Margouleff produced the album. David Sanborn plays alto and soprano saxophone, surrounded by a band that includes, among others, the bassist Marcus Miller, the drummer Omar Hakim, the guitarist Michael Sembello and the percussionist Paulinho da Costa.

Sembello himself sings lead vocals on two songs, Back Again and Love Will Come Someday, so the record also has a few vocal moments. George Duke plays clavinet on Port of Call, the opening track. The album reached number 70 on the Billboard 200, number 32 on the R&B albums chart and number 1 on Billboard's jazz albums chart.
werk/david-sanborn-as-we-speak.listen: Listen to Port of Call and notice the alto saxophone and the clavinet of George Duke.

werk/david-sanborn-backstreet.text:
Backstreet was released in 1983 and was produced by Marcus Miller, Michael Colina and Ray Bardani. Miller strongly shapes the sound: he plays piano, Fender Rhodes, synthesizers, vocoder, various guitars, bass, steel drums and timpani, and sings backing vocals. Colina plays piano, synthesizer and vocoder on four songs. The drummer Steve Gadd plays on two songs and Hiram Bullock on guitar on the first.

David Sanborn himself plays alto and soprano saxophone. On Neither One of Us, the closing track, we hear Ralph MacDonald on congas and percussion, and in the backing chorus, among others, Luther Vandross. On 27 January 1984 the album stood at number 1 on Billboard's traditional jazz albums chart.
werk/david-sanborn-backstreet.listen: Listen to Neither One of Us and notice the backing chorus, in which Luther Vandross, among others, sings.

werk/david-sanborn-taking-off.text:
Taking Off by the saxophonist David Sanborn was released in 1975 on Warner Bros. Records. John Court produced the album and Don Hahn was the engineer. It reached number 19 on Billboard's Jazz Albums chart.

The album contains nine songs by various composers. Unless otherwise stated they are by David Matthews. Steve Khan wrote Butterfat and Duck Ankles, Coleridge-Taylor Perkinson 'Way 'Cross Georgia, Don Grolnick The Whisperer and Randy Brecker It Took a Long Time. At six and a half minutes, Black Light is the longest track. Most of the other tracks last between three and five minutes, which gives the record a compact and varied character.
werk/david-sanborn-taking-off.listen: Listen to Butterfat and notice the saxophone. Try to hear how it relates to the rhythm section beneath it.

werk/david-sanborn-voyeur.text:
Voyeur is the sixth studio album by the alto saxophonist David Sanborn and was released in 1981 on Warner Bros. Well-known session musicians play on the record, among them the guitarist Hiram Bullock and the drummer Steve Gadd. The bassist and composer Marcus Miller plays a key role: he wrote some of the songs and provided the funky rhythms and colourful backdrops. The guitarist Buzz Feiten, who was attracting a lot of attention at the time with the Larsen-Feiten Band, adds his recognisable guitar sound to Let's Just Say Goodbye.

AllMusic calls the record an excellent example of the music of this highly influential saxophonist. The song All I Need Is You, written by Miller, won the 1982 Grammy for Best R&B Instrumental Performance. It was the first of seven Grammys the saxophonist has won so far.
werk/david-sanborn-voyeur.listen: In All I Need Is You, listen to the interplay between the alto saxophone and the funky rhythm section beneath it.

werk/de-dijk-mag-het-licht-uit.text: In 1987 Mag het licht uit by De Dijk from Amsterdam was released. The band chose American soul and rhythm and blues as its source, with horns and a tight rhythm section. The singer Huub van der Lubbe wrote lyrics about Amsterdam and the people who live there. De Dijk became one of the most popular live acts in the country. In 2010 the band even recorded an album with the American soul singer Solomon Burke.
werk/de-dijk-mag-het-licht-uit.listen: Hear the horns and the warmth of a soul ballad, with Huub van der Lubbe as the singer of the city.

werk/de-jeugd-van-tegenwoordig-watskebur.text: In 2005 Watskeburt?! was released, the first hit by De Jeugd van Tegenwoordig from Amsterdam. The song spent three weeks at number one in the Top 40. The group turned language into a playground, with invented words, street slang, absurd jokes and electronic beats. They knew the word watskeburt from Amsterdam street slang. After 2000, Nederhop grew into one of the most important genres in the country.

werk/de-la-soul-3-feet-high-and-rising.text:
3 Feet High and Rising was De La Soul's debut album and was released on 6 February 1989 on Tommy Boy Records. It was the first of three collaborations with the producer Prince Paul. The title is derived from the Johnny Cash song Five Feet High and Rising. While gangsta rap was on the rise, with hard and confrontational lyrics, this album opted for a playful, positive tone and strange subjects, from dandruff to gardening.

The production leans heavily on samples from funk and soul, but also from doo-wop, psychedelic rock and children's music. The skits in the form of a quiz show are also well known. The singles were Me Myself and I, The Magic Number, Buddy and Eye Know. Critics were enthusiastic and in The Village Voice's Pazz & Jop poll the album finished at number one in 1989. Because of concerns over the rights to the samples, it only appeared on streaming services in 2023.
werk/de-la-soul-3-feet-high-and-rising.listen: Listen to Me Myself and I and notice how light and playful it sounds compared with the hard rap of the time. Try to hear which familiar records are hidden beneath the beat.

werk/de-la-soul-aoi-bionix.text:
AOI: Bionix, De La Soul's sixth studio album, was released on 4 December 2001. It was the second part of a planned series of three discs and the group's last work for Tommy Boy. The first single, Baby Phat with Yummy Bingham and Devin the Dude, was an ode to fuller-figured women. In Held Down with Cee-Lo, Posdnuos reflects on fatherhood, religion and fame. Slick Rick takes part in What We Do (For Love), a funny song about puberty and sexual discovery.

Between the songs are sketches featuring Reverend Do Good, which also serve as social commentary. The last sketch leads into Peer Pressure, with J Dilla in the intro and outro. Tommy Boy ceased to exist, so the planned second single Special never came. The reviews were mostly favourable. Robert Christgau wrote that anyone wondering what hip hop sounds like when it grows up will find the answer here.
werk/de-la-soul-aoi-bionix.listen: Listen to Held Down and notice how Posdnuos reflects on fatherhood, religion and fame.

werk/de-la-soul-art-official-intelligenc.text:
On 8 August 2000 De La Soul's fifth studio album was released. It was the first part of a planned series of three discs. Many guests take part: Redman, Tash and J-Ro of Tha Liks, Xzibit, Busta Rhymes, Mike D and Ad Rock of the Beastie Boys, Busy Bee, Freddie Foxxx and Chaka Khan. More than half of the album features a guest. Unlike its predecessor Stakes Is High, it brought the group back into the charts, thanks to the singles Oooh. and All Good?. The album was nominated for a Grammy.

Oooh. uses replayed elements from Enter the Dragon by Lalo Schifrin, and U Can Do (Life) contains a sample of Le Freak by Chic. The reviews were positive. Robert Christgau wrote that the old jokers had grown into the purest musicians in hip hop, with art in beats, flow and melodies. In the United States the album entered at number 9.
werk/de-la-soul-art-official-intelligenc.listen: Listen to Oooh. and notice how Redman joins in as a guest and which replayed elements lie beneath the song.

werk/de-la-soul-de-la-soul-is-dead.text:
After the celebrated debut 3 Feet High and Rising, many listeners eagerly awaited a second record. De La Soul chose a different direction. The title and the cover, with a broken pot of daisies, are a farewell to the hippie image of the D.A.I.S.Y. age. The producer Prince Paul said they wanted to prove they did not have just one album in them. The album was released on 14 May 1991. A series of skits parodies old read-along books with records, in which bullies steal a cassette with an album by the group and criticise it.

The humour is darker and more cynical than before. My Brother's a Basehead is about addiction, Millie Pulled a Pistol on Santa about sexual abuse. In contrast there are lighthearted songs such as A Roller Skating Jam Named Saturdays. The reviews were divided, but the music received more praise than the tone. The magazine The Source was one of the first to give the album its top rating of five mics.
werk/de-la-soul-de-la-soul-is-dead.listen: Listen to Ring Ring Ring (Ha Ha Hey) and notice the contrast between the lyrics, in which the group complains about up-and-coming artists who want to hitch a ride, and the playful disco groove beneath.

werk/de-la-soul-stakes-is-high.text:
Stakes Is High is De La Soul's fourth album and was released on 2 July 1996 on Tommy Boy Records. For the first time the group did not work with Prince Paul: the production he delivered did not, according to the group, suit the mood of the record. Most of it was produced by the three themselves, with extra tracks by Jay Dee, DJ Ogee, Spearhead X and Skeff Anslem.

The album is regarded as the group's darkest and most serious. It deals with the state of hip hop, the commercialisation of hip hop culture and criticism of gangsta rap. Mos Def reached a wider audience through Big Brother Beat and Common appears on The Bizness. Between the songs are audio clips, such as people telling where they were when they first heard Criminal Minded. The reviews were mostly strong, though sales disappointed. Robert Christgau wrote that it was a relief that the group was back.
werk/de-la-soul-stakes-is-high.listen: Listen to the intro and notice the clips in which people tell where they were when they first heard Criminal Minded.

werk/dead-or-alive-mad-bad-and-dangerous.text:
In December 1986 the third studio album by the English pop band Dead or Alive was released on Epic Records. The group again worked with the production team Stock Aitken Waterman, and that yielded hit singles, among them Brand New Lover and Something in My House. The collaboration was not always enjoyable. The producers wanted the band to focus on house, and the singer Pete Burns did not want to leave the songwriting to them. There were fierce arguments in the studio, although engineers later said the atmosphere was mostly businesslike and sometimes even amusing.

The cover, too, tells a story. Next to Burns stands one of the walls of the Château de Raray, where scenes for the 1946 film La Belle et la Bête were shot. The title is a remark made by Lady Caroline Lamb about the poet Lord Byron.
werk/dead-or-alive-mad-bad-and-dangerous.listen: Listen to Something in My House, at over seven minutes the longest track on the album. Notice how the song is given time to develop.

werk/dead-or-alive-sophisticated-boom-bo.text:
Sophisticated Boom Boom is the debut album of the English group Dead or Alive, released on 20 April 1984 by Epic Records. Zeus B. Held produced it, and Pete Burns sang. The title comes from a song by the Shangri-Las, and the cover, photographed by Peter Ashworth, was inspired by Lionheart by Kate Bush. The working title Mad, Bad and Dangerous to Know was rejected by the label.

The music is mostly synth-pop with danceable elements. The album contains the band's first British top forty single, a cover of That's the Way (I Like It) by KC and the Sunshine Band. That song and Misty Circles did well on the American dance chart. In the United Kingdom the album reached number 29. The cassette version had three extra songs.
werk/dead-or-alive-sophisticated-boom-bo.listen: Listen to That's the Way (I Like It) and notice how a disco classic acquires a new atmosphere through synthesizers and danceable rhythms.

werk/dead-or-alive-youthquake.text:
Youthquake is the second studio album by the English pop band Dead or Alive and was released on 13 May 1985 on Epic Records. It was the first time the band worked with the production team Stock Aitken Waterman. The recording sessions were tense: there were clashes between band and producers, and according to the engineer Phil Harding it almost came to blows.

The sound consists of tight sequencers, drum machines and synthesizers, with Pete Burns's dramatic vocals on top. The album broke through in Europe and the United States thanks to You Spin Me Round (Like a Record), which reached number 1 in England. Lover Come Back to Me, In Too Deep and My Heart Goes Bang (Get Me to the Doctor) were also released as singles. The reception was mixed. Smash Hits praised the danceable songs but found the production too cold, while Rolling Stone was negative.
werk/dead-or-alive-youthquake.listen: Listen to You Spin Me Round (Like a Record) and notice the drum machine and the sequencers: how do they hold the tempo tight beneath Pete Burns's vocals?

werk/deep-purple-deep-purple-in-rock.text:
In 1969 the band had made three albums, but lacked a clear direction. After hearing Led Zeppelin's debut, the guitarist Ritchie Blackmore wanted to play really heavy. The singer Rod Evans was replaced by Ian Gillan, and the bassist Roger Glover joined. This is how the Mark II line-up came about, which played on this album for the first time. The group rehearsed in a community centre in Hanwell, because a lot of noise was allowed there. The recording sessions in London ran from October to April, in between gigs.

The music had to sound hard and heavy and to capture the group's live sound. Child in Time and Speed King had already grown on stage. The album became the breakthrough in Europe and reached number four in the United Kingdom. In the United States it did less well. It is still praised as an important early example of hard rock and heavy metal.
werk/deep-purple-deep-purple-in-rock.listen: Listen to Child in Time and notice how the song builds step by step from a quiet beginning to something much heavier.

werk/deep-purple-fireball.text:
After the success of In Rock, Deep Purple had to make a follow-up, in the Mark II line-up of Jon Lord, Ritchie Blackmore, Ian Paice, Roger Glover and Ian Gillan. All the concerts caused the group health problems: Lord suffered with his back, Glover with his stomach, and Blackmore and Gillan fell into conflict. The recording was done between tours, from September 1970 to June 1971. The first session yielded only Anyone's Daughter. The Mule came about at Welcombe Manor in Devon and Demon's Eye was the last to be recorded.

In the United States the album was released in July 1971, with Strange Kind of Woman in place of Demon's Eye. In Britain in September it became the first of the band's three number 1 albums. The title song reached number 15 as a single.
werk/deep-purple-fireball.listen: Listen to Fireball and notice the drumming of Ian Paice, who used a double bass drum for it.

werk/deep-purple-machine-head.text:
Machine Head was preceded by a period of heavy touring. Earlier albums had been recorded between concerts, and the band felt that those records did not sound as good as its live performances. It therefore chose to record outside an ordinary studio, in December 1971 in Montreux, with the Rolling Stones' mobile studio. The casino where they were due to work burned down during a Frank Zappa concert, when someone fired a flare into the ceiling. In the end the group converted the closed Grand Hotel into a recording space.

That fire became the subject of Smoke on the Water. The bassist Roger Glover woke up with the title in his head, and Ian Gillan wrote the lyrics about the events. The group had already played Highway Star and Lazy on tour. Machine Head became Deep Purple's most commercially successful record, reached number one in several countries and is regarded as an important link in the development of heavy metal.
werk/deep-purple-machine-head.listen: Listen to Smoke on the Water and notice how the famous guitar riff begins alone at first and is then joined by bass and drums.

werk/deep-purple-the-book-of-taliesyn.text:
The Book of Taliesyn is Deep Purple's second album, recorded only three months after the debut. The label Tetragrammaton wanted a new record for the first American tour, so in August 1968 the band went to De Lane Lea Studios in London, with the producer Derek Lawrence. There were four long original songs and three adapted covers. The sound mixes psychedelic rock, progressive rock and hard rock, with classical influences from the keyboardist Jon Lord.

Anthem goes furthest in that classical direction, with a Baroque string quartet as an interlude. Wring That Neck is a heavy instrumental, and Kentucky Woman an adaptation of a hit by Neil Diamond. In America the record reached number 54. In the United Kingdom it appeared in 1969 as the first release on Harvest Records and went almost unnoticed.
werk/deep-purple-the-book-of-taliesyn.listen: In Anthem, listen to the Baroque interlude with string quartet in the middle of the song.

werk/deftones-adrenaline.text:
Stephen Carpenter, Abe Cunningham and Chino Moreno were school friends in Sacramento and began playing together around 1988 in Carpenter's garage. Later the bassist Chi Cheng joined. Adrenaline, their debut, was released on 3 October 1995 on Maverick Records. Terry Date produced most of it; the hidden track Fist came from Ross Robinson. The band recorded the record quickly, and Moreno sang all his parts live in the same room as the band.

The music is described as nu metal, post-hardcore and alternative metal. Singles were 7 Words and Bored. Critics compared the band with, among others, Helmet, Korn and Nine Inch Nails and praised the new sound. AllMusic called the group controlled, even in the midst of chaos, and The Rough Guide to Heavy Metal counts the record among the best examples of nu metal.
werk/deftones-adrenaline.listen: In Lifter, listen to the sharp guitar of Stephen Carpenter and notice how tight it sounds.

werk/deftones-around-the-fur.text:
For their second album Deftones moved to Seattle in 1997. From April to June they recorded at Studio Litho, which belongs to Stone Gossard of Pearl Jam. The four band members rented an apartment in South Seattle while they wrote and recorded. Terry Date produced again, and this time the band wanted to sound more refined. Cunningham used a different snare drum on almost every song. Max Cavalera of Sepultura sings along on Headup.

Around the Fur was released on 28 October 1997 on Maverick. Critics praised the shifts between soft and hard, the good sequencing of the songs and Moreno's distinctive vocals. The singles My Own Summer (Shove It) and Be Quiet and Drive (Far Away) received a lot of airplay and were also played on MTV. In 1998 the record won a Kerrang! Award for best album.
werk/deftones-around-the-fur.listen: In Headup, listen to the extra vocals of Max Cavalera alongside those of Chino Moreno.

werk/deftones-deftones.text:
Deftones is the fourth studio album by the American alternative metal band and was released on 20 May 2003 on Maverick Records. It was the last record with the producer Terry Date until Ohms in 2020. With costs of 2.5 million dollars, it is among the most expensive albums ever made. Many songs revolve around guitarist Stephen Carpenter's low G# tuning.

Still, it is a versatile album. Lucky You is a dark, soft trip-hop piece with DJ Crook and the singer Rey Osburn. In Anniversary of an Uninteresting Event a grand piano and a toy piano can be heard. Minerva is known as a shoegaze song. The reception was divided: Rolling Stone was enthusiastic, Pitchfork negative, and the album did less well than White Pony. The singer Chino Moreno said in 2020 that he himself was dissatisfied with the record.
werk/deftones-deftones.listen: Listen to Minerva and notice how heavy guitars and a dreamy, layered sound come together in the same song.

werk/deftones-saturday-night-wrist.text:
Saturday Night Wrist was released on 31 October 2006 on Maverick Records and was the result of more than two hard years. After the lukewarm reception of the 2003 album, the band had to write again, first in Sacramento and then in Malibu. Several producers came by: Dan the Automator, for a week, and then Bob Ezrin with Brian Virtue. Tensions rose and the singer Chino Moreno, who was struggling with addictions and a failing marriage, temporarily stepped out of the sessions. In early 2006 all the recorded vocals went into the bin and Shaun Lopez took over the production.

Annie Hardy of Giant Drag and Serj Tankian of System of a Down play on the album. Tankian also co-wrote Mein. Fans and critics responded positively, some finding it better than its predecessor. Moreno himself calls it his least favourite album by the band.
werk/deftones-saturday-night-wrist.listen: Listen to Mein and try to hear the contribution of Serj Tankian of System of a Down, who co-wrote the song.

werk/deftones-white-pony.text:
White Pony was recorded at The Plant Recording Studios in Sausalito, with the producer Terry Date, who had also made the first two albums. The band worked in the studio for four months, longer than ever, and took their time, even though there was pressure to release sooner. Frank Delgado became a permanent member for the first time, on turntables and synthesizer, and Chino Moreno played rhythm guitar for the first time. Moreno did not write about himself, but devised storylines.

Deftones' third album added influences from post-hardcore, trip hop, shoegaze, progressive rock and post-rock to alternative metal. Change (In the House of Flies) was the first single and became a radio hit; Elite won a Grammy for Best Metal Performance in 2001. On Passenger, Maynard James Keenan of Tool sings along. Critics see the record as a turning point: NPR Music spoke of a new direction for heavy and experimental music.
werk/deftones-white-pony.listen: Listen to Passenger and notice the interplay between the voices of Chino Moreno and Maynard James Keenan, with piano and keyboard beneath, before heavy guitars launch the choruses.

werk/demis-roussos-forever-and-ever.text:
Forever and Ever is the second studio album by the Greek singer and songwriter Demis Roussos. It was released in 1973 on Philips Records and was a great success: it topped the album charts of Germany, the Netherlands and Norway and reached number two in Austria.

On the record play, among others, Orphe on bouzouki, Jean-Jacques Cramier on twelve-string guitar, Chris Hayward on flute and Stelios Vlavianos on organ and Moog synthesizer. There are also two trombonists, Alex Perdigon and G. Conti. The backing vocals are credited to all the friends. Roger Roche was the engineer and Bernard Leloup took the photograph for the cover.
werk/demis-roussos-forever-and-ever.listen: In Forever and Ever, listen to the vocals and try to recognise the instruments that sound around them.

werk/depeche-mode-a-broken-frame.text:
At the end of 1981 Vince Clarke, the main writer, left the group to form Yazoo. The remaining three, Martin Gore, Andrew Fletcher and Dave Gahan, carried on at Blackwing Studios with the producer Daniel Miller. Gore wrote the album entirely alone, partly with songs from his teenage years. The first song, See You, reached number six in England. Alan Wilder joined as a touring musician, but did not yet play on the record. The sound is varied: light pop songs such as A Photograph of You and more mature work such as The Sun and the Rainfall. Leave in Silence is darker and more experimental. For the first time the band used samples, such as marching boots in Shouldn't Have Done That.

The album reached number eight in England. Three singles made the top twenty.
werk/depeche-mode-a-broken-frame.listen: Listen to Shouldn't Have Done That and notice the sound of marching boots: how is this sampled sound worked into the music?

werk/depeche-mode-construction-time-agai.text:
Construction Time Again is Depeche Mode's third studio album and was released on 22 August 1983 on Mute Records. Alan Wilder took part as a band member for the first time and wrote two songs. For the first time the band did not record at Blackwing Studios but at The Garden, John Foxx's studio in London, with Gareth Jones as engineer. Mixing took place at Hansa Studios in West Berlin.

Martin Gore wrote the songs quickly, after travels on which the poverty in Thailand had shocked the band. Together with Daniel Miller the group switched from analogue synthesizers to sampling. They recorded found sounds: metal they struck with sledgehammers, kitchen utensils and objects from building sites. This gave the pop music an industrial edge, partly because of Gore's interest in Einstürzende Neubauten. The album title comes from a line in the song Pipeline.
werk/depeche-mode-construction-time-agai.listen: Listen to Pipeline: the vocals were recorded at a spot next to railway lines at Shoreditch, so notice the trains and other ambient sounds in the background.

werk/depeche-mode-music-for-the-masses.text:
After Black Celebration, Depeche Mode entered the studio in late 1986 without the producer Daniel Miller and without Gareth Jones. Alan Wilder took the lead in the production, with David Bascombe as an outside producer who mainly worked as engineer. Recording began at Studio Guillaume Tell near Paris and continued at Konk in London. The band made many new samples in the studio, including with an old grand piano and orchestral drums. There is also more guitar. Martin Gore wrote the basic songs, Wilder worked out the arrangements.

The sound is grand and dramatic, with a lot of reverb. The singer Dave Gahan spoke of electronic metal, and said they had discovered dynamics. Strangelove, Never Let Me Down Again, Behind the Wheel and Little 15 became singles. With his videos, Anton Corbijn defined the group's new look. The record helped the band break through in America, and the tour ended at the Rose Bowl before more than 70,000 fans.
werk/depeche-mode-music-for-the-masses.listen: Listen to Never Let Me Down Again and notice how the band builds tension and releases it again, with a lot of space and reverb in the sound.
